author: Anthony Pettitt
text: A Gaussian conditional autoregressive (CAR) formulation is presented that permits the modelling of the spatial dependence and the dependence between multivariate random variables at irregularly spaced sites so capturing some of the modelling advantages of the geostatistical approach. The model benefits not only from the explicit availability of the full conditionals but also from the computational simplicity of the precision matrix determinant calculation using a closed form expression involving the eigenvalues of a precision matrix submatrix. The introduction of covariates into the model adds little computational complexity to the analysis and thus the method can be straightforwardly extended to regression models. The model, because of its computational simplicity, is well suited to application involving the fully Bayesian analysis of large data sets involving multivariate measurements with a spatial ordering. An extension to spatio-temporal data is also considered. Here, we demonstrate use of the model in the analysis of bivariate binary data where the observed data is modelled as the sign of the hidden CAR process. A case study involving over 450 irregularly spaced sites and the presence or absence of each of two species of rain forest trees at each site is presented; Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods are implemented to obtain posterior distributions of all unknowns. The MCMC method works well with simulated data and the tree biodiversity data set.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: Bayesian inference has commonly been performed on nonlinear mixed effects models. However, there is a lack of research into performing Bayesian optimal design for nonlinear mixed effects models, especially those that require searches to be performed over several design variables. This is likely due to the fact that it is much more computationally intensive to perform optimal experimental design for nonlinear mixed effects models than it is to perform inference in the Bayesian framework. Fully Bayesian experimental designs for nonlinear mixed effects models are presented, which involve the use of simulation-based optimal design methods to search over both continuous and discrete design spaces. The design problem is to determine the optimal number of subjects and samples per subject, as well as the (near) optimal urine sampling times for a population pharmacokinetic study in horses, so that the population pharmacokinetic parameters can be precisely estimated, subject to cost constraints. The optimal sampling strategies, in terms of the number of subjects and the number of samples per subject, were found to be substantially different between the examples considered in this work, which highlights the fact that the designs are rather problem-dependent and can be addressed using the methods presented. (C) 2015 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: Motor unit number estimation (MUNE) is a method which aims to provide a quantitative indicator of progression of diseases that lead to a loss of motor units, such as motor neurone disease. However the development of a reliable, repeatable and fast real-time MUNE method has proved elusive hitherto. Previously, a reversible jump Markov chain Monte Carlo (RJMCMC) algorithm has been implemented to produce a posterior distribution for the number of motor units using a Bayesian hierarchical model that takes into account biological information about motor unit activation. However this approach can be unreliable for some datasets since it can suffer from poor cross-dimensional mixing. The focus is on improved inference by marginalising over latent variables to create the likelihood. More specifically, the emphasis is on how this marginalisation can improve the RJMCMC mixing and that alternative approaches that utilise the likelihood (e.g. DIC) can be investigated. For this model the marginalisation is over latent variables which, for a larger number of motor units, is an intractable summation over all combinations of a set of latent binary variables whose joint sample space increases exponentially with the number of motor units. A tractable and accurate approximation for this quantity is provided and also other approximations based on Monte Carlo estimates that can be incorporated into RJMCMC are investigated. (C) 2013 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: The issue of modelling non-Gaussian time series data is one that has been examined by several authors in recent years. Zeger(1988) introduced a parameter-driven model for a time series of counts as well as a more general observation-driven model for non-Gaussian data (Zeger Qaqish, 1988). This paper examines the application of the added variable plot to these two models. This plot is useful for determining the strength of relationships and the detection of influential or outlying observations.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: Cramér-von Mises type statistics are modified so that they can be used to test the goodness of fit of a censored sample, when the distribution function is known completely. Asymptotic percentage points are given, small-sample applications are discussed and asymptotic power considered.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: In this paper we present a sequential Monte Carlo algorithm for Bayesian sequential experimental design applied to generalised non-linear models for discrete data. The approach is computationally convenient in that the information of newly observed data can be incorporated through a simple re-weighting step. We also consider a flexible parametric model for the stimulus-response relationship together with a newly developed hybrid design utility that can produce more robust estimates of the target stimulus in the presence of substantial model and parameter uncertainty. The algorithm is applied to hypothetical clinical trial or bioassay scenarios. In the discussion, potential generalisations of the algorithm are suggested to possibly extend its applicability to a wide variety of scenarios. (C) 2012 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: The autologistic model is commonly used to model spatial binary data on the lattice. However, if the lattice size is too large, then exact calculation of its normalizing constant poses a major difficulty. Various different methods for estimation of model parameters, such as pseudo-likelihood, have been proposed to overcome this problem. This article presents a method to estimate the normalizing constant in an efficient manner. In particular, this allows tasks such as maximum likelihood estimation and inference for model parameters. We also consider the true likelihood approximated by the product of likelihoods for which the normalizing constant can be found by an analytic computational method by wrapping the lattice on the cylinder. This gives a simulation-free method of inference. We compare estimates of model parameters based on our new methods with the commonly used pseudo-likelihood approach. Although we have not considered Bayesian inferences here, the method can be straightforwardly extended to find posterior distributions. We apply our methods to the well-known endive data and to simulated data and find that our methods give substantially increased accuracy of estimation of model parameters.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: A number of statistical tests have been recommended over the last twenty years for assessing the randomness of long binary strings used in cryptographic algorithms. Several of these tests include methods of examining subblock patterns. These tests are the uniformity test, the universal test and the repetition test. The effectiveness of these tests are compared based on the subblock length, the limitations on data requirements, and on their power in detecting deviations from randomness. Due to the complexity of the test statistics, the power functions are estimated by simulation methods. The results show that for small subblocks the uniformity test is more powerful than the universal test, and that there is some doubt about the parameters of the hypothesised distribution for the universal test statistic. For larger subblocks the results show that the repetition test is the most effective test, since it requires far less data than either of the other two tests and is an efficient test in detecting deviations from randomness in binary strings.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: Dose-finding designs estimate the dose level of a drug based on observed adverse events. Relatedness of the adverse event to the drug has been generally ignored in all proposed design methodologies. These designs assume that the adverse events observed during a trial are definitely related to the drug, which can lead to flawed dose-level estimation. We incorporate adverse event relatedness into the so-called continual reassessment method. Adverse events that have doubtful' or possible' relationships to the drug are modelled using a two-parameter logistic model with an additive probability mass. Adverse events probably' or definitely' related to the drug are modelled using a cumulative logistic model. To search for the maximum tolerated dose, we use the maximum estimated toxicity probability of these two adverse event relatedness categories. We conduct a simulation study that illustrates the characteristics of the design under various scenarios. This article demonstrates that adverse event relatedness is important for improved dose estimation. It opens up further research pathways into continual reassessment design methodologies. Copyright (c) 2013 John Wiley Sons, Ltd.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: Biological data are frequently collected with small numbers of observations from several subjects. Often a linear model is fitted to the data by averaging over subjects. Frequently there are considerable between-subject differences, and due allowance should be made for these when the model is fitted by parametric techniques. In this paper it is proposed that the model should be fitted by using the within-subject ranks of the observations. The technique is applied to the problem of estimating the cosinor' diagram for biological rhythm data. An example involving melatonin levels, in which there are considerable between-subject differences, is considered. The results obtained by use of the ranks are compared with those of a parametric analysis which makes allowance for the between-subject differences. The results are very similar, but the rank analysis requires much less computation.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: A new method for estimating the time to colonization of Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus Aureus (MRSA) patients is developed in this paper. The time to colonization of MRSA is modelled using a Bayesian smoothing approach for the hazard function. There are two prior models discussed in this paper: the first difference prior and the second difference prior. The second difference prior model gives smoother estimates of the hazard functions and, when applied to data from an intensive care unit (ICU), clearly shows increasing hazard up to day 13, then a decreasing hazard. The results clearly demonstrate that the hazard is not constant and provide a useful quantification of the effect of length of stay on the risk of MRSA colonization which provides useful insight. Copyright (C) 2004 John Wiley Sons, Ltd.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: The problem of testing for bivariate normality using the empirical distribution function is considered. A Cram r-von Mises type statistic is defined and asymptotic percentage points for this statistic given. This involves solving a two-dimensional homogeneous integral equation. Unfortunately the Cram r-von Mises statistic is not invariant under orthogonal transformations of the data so that an invariant statistic is developed. Approximations for the distribution of this statistic are found by Monte Carlo. Applications of the statistics are given. It is shown that the statistics are particularly sensitive to certain kinds of pattern in the data and they could be useful in data analysis apart from providing a formal test of bivariate normality

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: Phase-type distributions represent the time to absorption for a finite state Markov chain in continuous time, generalising the exponential distribution and providing a flexible and useful modelling tool. We present a new reversible jump Markov chain Monte Carlo scheme for performing a fully Bayesian analysis of the popular Coxian subclass of phase-type models: the convenient Coxian representation involves fewer parameters than a more general phase-type model. The key novelty of our approach is that we model covariate dependence in the mean whilst using the Coxian phase-type model as a very general residual distribution. Such incorporation of covariates into the model has not previously been attempted in the Bayesian literature. A further novelty is that we also propose a reversible jump scheme for investigating structural changes to the model brought about by the introduction of Erlang phases. Our approach addresses more questions of inference than previous Bayesian treatments of this model and is automatic in nature. We analyse an example clataset comprising lengths of hospital stays of a sample of patients collected from two Australian hospitals to produce a model for a patient's expected length of stay which incorporates the effects of several covariates. This leads to interesting conclusions about what contributes to length of hospital stay with implications for hospital planning. We compare our results with an alternative classical analysis of these data. (C) 2009 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: The binary derivative has been used to measure the randomness of a binary string formed by a pseudorandom number generator for use in cipher systems. In this paper we develop statistical properties of the binary derivative and show that certain types of randomness testing in binary derivatives are equivalent to well-established tests for randomness in the original string. A uniform method of testing randomness in binary strings is described based on using the binary derivative. We show that the new tests are faster and more powerful than several of the well-established tests for randomness.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: In this paper, we introduce a novel statistical framework based on a Conditional Autoregressive Gaussian Process (CAGP) designed to address the challenges posed by irregularly spaced multivariate data, particularly in the context of modeling large datasets with binary outcomes. Traditional approaches to multivariate binary data often assume regular spacing and normality, which limits their applicability in practical scenarios where data collection intervals are inconsistent. Our proposed method extends classical Gaussian processes by incorporating a conditional autoregressive structure, enabling the effective capture of temporal dependencies and interactions across multiple variables, even when observations are missing or unevenly distributed. We provide a comprehensive theoretical foundation for the CAGP, detailing its construction and parameter estimation via a Bayesian framework. To illustrate the utility of our model, we apply it to a large set of ecological data, demonstrating its effectiveness in modeling species presence-absence measures over varying spatial and temporal scales. Through simulations and real data applications, we showcase the advantages of our approach over existing methodologies, emphasizing improved predictive performance and uncertainty quantification. Our findings highlight the potential of CAGP in advancing the statistical modeling of complex datasets across diverse scientific fields.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: In this paper, we propose a novel simulation-based fully Bayesian approach for experimental design tailored to mixed effects models. Mixed effects models are pivotal in various fields where both fixed and random effects influence the response variable, yet traditional design methodologies often fall short in effectively capturing model uncertainty and variability. Our method leverages advanced simulation techniques to generate posterior distributions of key parameters, facilitating the exploration of design alternatives in a Bayesian framework. We illustrate the process of developing optimal experimental designs that minimize expected loss while accounting for both the fixed effects that characterize average population behavior and the random effects that encapsulate individual-level variation. Through simulation studies, we demonstrate the robustness of our approach relative to classical design strategies, showcasing its effectiveness in providing more accurate parameter estimates and enhancing the efficiency of data collection. Additionally, we discuss practical implications for practitioners, including software implementation for real-world applications. Our findings highlight the advantage of a fully Bayesian paradigm in experimental design, paving the way for more informed and flexible decision-making in the study of complex systems governed by mixed effects.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: In this paper, we present a novel statistical approach that integrates Marginal Reversible Jump Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MRJ-MCMC) techniques for the estimation of motor unit numbers in electrophysiological studies. Traditional methods for assessing motor unit number rely on restrictive assumptions around model parameters, which can lead to biased inferences. Our MRJ-MCMC framework enhances the flexibility of model selection by allowing the number of parameters to change across iterations, thus accommodating varying complexities in the underlying data structure. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by applying it to simulated datasets and real-world electromyographic data. Our results reveal significant improvements in parameter estimation accuracy and uncertainty quantification compared to conventional methods. Additionally, we provide a thorough discussion on the implementation details, including convergence diagnostics and computational considerations. This work not only advances methodologies in motor unit estimation but also contributes to the broader field of Bayesian statistical modeling, offering a versatile tool for researchers analyzing hierarchical and mixed models.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: This paper explores the application of added variable plots (AVPs) in the context of time series data characterized by counts, a common feature in various fields such as epidemiology, economics, and environmental studies. Traditional regression diagnostics often rely on residual analysis to assess model fit and identify influential observations; however, the unique challenges posed by count data such as non-negativity, overdispersion, and temporal dependence require tailored approaches. We present a methodological framework for constructing and interpreting added variable plots specifically designed for count time series, which allow researchers to visualize the effect of individual predictors while accounting for the dynamic structure inherent in the data. Through simulation studies and real-world case applications, we demonstrate how these plots can reveal crucial insights into the relationships between predictors and response variables, as well as assist in identifying potential model misspecification. Our findings highlight the utility of AVPs as a complementary diagnostic tool in time series analysis of count data, paving the way for more robust and informative statistical modeling practices.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text:
**Abstract** 

This paper introduces a modified version of the Cramér-von Mises statistic tailored for analyzing censored data, a common scenario in survival analysis and reliability testing. Traditional Cramér-von Mises tests, while effective for complete data sets, face limitations when applied to censored observations, potentially leading to biased estimations and invalid inference. Our proposed modification addresses these challenges by adapting the original statistic to accommodate right-censored, left-censored, and interval-censored data while maintaining its asymptotic properties. We derive the new test's distribution under the null hypothesis and demonstrate its consistency and efficiency through extensive simulation studies. The performance of the modified statistic is compared against traditional approaches, showing improvements in both power and robustness under varying censoring mechanisms. A practical application in clinical trial data illustrates the utility of our method in real-world scenarios. This work enhances statistical methodologies for censored data analysis and offers a reliable tool for researchers in fields requiring accurate assessment of survival outcomes.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: In this paper, we present a novel application of Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) methods tailored for Bayesian sequentially designed experiments involving discrete data. As experimental design increasingly relies on Bayesian principles to optimize data collection and analysis, traditional approaches often struggle with the complexities introduced by sequentiality and discrete outcomes. Our method integrates SMC techniques to enhance the efficiency of updating posterior distributions in real-time as new data points are acquired. We develop a framework that allows for dynamic adaptation of experimental conditions based on observed outcomes, facilitating informed decision-making throughout the study. Through a series of simulation studies, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in various discrete data scenarios, highlighting improvements in accuracy and convergence rates compared to conventional updating techniques. Our results suggest that SMC can significantly streamline the design and execution of Bayesian experiments, paving the way for more responsive and data-driven research methodologies in various fields, including clinical trials and social sciences.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: The autologistic model is a prominent framework for analyzing binary spatial data, capturing the influence of neighboring observations while accommodating inherent spatial dependencies. This paper presents a comprehensive approach to the likelihood estimation and statistical inference for the autologistic model, detailing both parametric and non-parametric estimation techniques. We derive the likelihood function based on a latent variable representation, enabling efficient computation through the use of numerical optimization methods. Additionally, we propose a robust framework for hypothesis testing and confidence interval construction, employing likelihood ratio tests and bootstrapping methods to address the complexities of spatial data. Through extensive simulation studies, we demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of our proposed estimators and inference procedures under varying conditions of spatial correlation and data sparsity. Finally, we apply our methodology to a real-world dataset, illustrating the practical implications of the autologistic model in ecological and social sciences. Our findings contribute to the existing literature by enhancing the understanding of spatial dependencies in binary outcomes and providing a reliable tool for researchers in various fields.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: In statistical analysis, identifying and testing for specific patterns within subblocks of data plays a critical role in various fields, including genetics, finance, and social sciences. This paper presents a comprehensive framework for testing subblock patterns, characterized by their unique structural features and underlying dependencies. We introduce novel statistical methods tailored to detect both predefined and emerging patterns within subblocks, employing a combination of hypothesis testing, permutation methods, and multivariate regression techniques. Our approach accounts for the heterogeneity of data distributions and allows for adjustments in the presence of confounding variables. We provide theoretical derivations to ensure the robustness and efficacy of our proposed methods, followed by a series of simulations that illustrate their performance compared to existing techniques. Additionally, we apply our methods to real-world datasets, demonstrating their utility in uncovering significant subblock patterns that may have gone undetected. The results underscore the relevance of the proposed methodologies in enhancing pattern recognition in complex datasets, setting a foundation for future research in adaptive statistical modeling and analysis.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: In the realm of dose-finding clinical trials, the accurate assessment of drug safety and efficacy is paramount. This paper introduces a novel statistical framework that incorporates the concept of adverse event relatedness into traditional dose-finding designs. We propose an adaptive trial methodology that quantifies the relationship between doses administered and the occurrence of adverse events, facilitating a more nuanced understanding of safety profiles. By integrating relatedness data categorizing adverse events based on their plausible connection to the treatment into Bayesian hierarchical models, we enhance both the estimation of optimal dose levels and the identification of doses that minimize adverse outcomes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through simulation studies and real-world case scenarios, highlighting its potential to improve decision-making in clinical development. The findings suggest that accounting for adverse event relatedness can lead to more efficient dose selection and ultimately enhance patient safety. Our work lays the groundwork for future research on adaptive clinical trial designs that prioritize both therapeutic benefits and safety considerations.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: Biological rhythms, such as circadian cycles, are fundamental to the functioning of living organisms and often exhibit periodic patterns that can be modeled using sinusoidal functions. Traditional methods of fitting sinusoidal models to biological data typically rely on least squares regression, which can be sensitive to outliers and non-normal data distributions. This paper presents a robust alternative approach that utilizes rank-based statistical techniques to fit sinusoidal models to biological rhythm data. We propose a rank-based fitting method that minimizes the ranks of the residuals rather than their raw values, effectively reducing the influence of outliers and enhancing robustness. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method through simulations and empirical applications using circadian rhythm datasets. Our results indicate that the rank-based sinusoidal fitting not only improves the accuracy of the parameter estimates but also provides better visual representations of biological rhythms. The findings suggest that incorporating rank-based approaches for sinusoidal fitting can substantially enhance the analysis of biological time series data, leading to more reliable interpretations of rhythm dynamics. Furthermore, we provide an R package that facilitates the implementation of our method for researchers in the field.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: The increasing prevalence of Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) colonization in intensive care units (ICUs) poses significant challenges for infection control and patient management. This study presents a novel statistical approach for smoothing discrete hazard functions to analyze the number of patients colonized with MRSA in an ICU setting. Utilizing a dataset collected over a one-year period, we applied non-parametric smoothing techniques to estimate the hazard function of MRSA colonization, allowing for more robust inference regarding temporal trends and potential risk factors. By employing kernel smoothing and local regression methods, we mitigated the effects of data sparsity and noise typically observed in discrete count data. Our findings reveal distinct temporal patterns in MRSA colonization rates and highlight key periods of increased risk, providing valuable insights for infection prevention strategies. Additionally, this work demonstrates the effectiveness of smoothing techniques in enhancing the interpretability of hazard functions in the context of public health surveillance. The results underscore the importance of ongoing monitoring and tailored intervention measures to curb the spread of MRSA in ICUs.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: Assessing the bivariate normality of data sets is crucial in many statistical applications, including multivariate analysis and regression modeling. Traditional methods for testing normality often rely on parametric assumptions, which may not hold in practice. This paper presents a novel testing procedure for bivariate normality that utilizes the empirical distribution function (EDF). By leveraging the EDF's ability to capture the joint distribution of the observations, we propose a statistic based on the Kolmogorov-Smirnov framework adapted for the bivariate case. The proposed method is evaluated through extensive simulations, demonstrating its robustness against deviations from normality and its superior performance compared to existing tests. We also provide a consistent bootstrap approach to enhance the power of our test when applied to finite sample sizes. Finally, the practical applicability of our method is illustrated through real-world data examples, reinforcing the EDF's effectiveness as a tool for assessing bivariate normality. Our findings contribute to the toolkit available for practitioners facing the challenges of multivariate data analysis.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: In this paper, we propose a fully Bayesian framework for the inference of Coxian phase-type distributions that incorporate covariate-dependent means. Phase-type distributions are widely utilized in various fields, including queuing theory and reliability analysis, due to their flexibility in modeling complex time-to-event data. However, traditional methods often fail to account for the influence of covariates on the distribution parameters. Our approach leverages Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods to posterior sampling, allowing us to integrate covariate effects into the Coxian phase-type structure seamlessly. We develop a prior specification that accommodates the hierarchical nature of the model, enhancing its robustness against overfitting. Through extensive simulation studies, we demonstrate the efficacy of our Bayesian framework in accurately estimating parameters and making predictions in scenarios with varying complexity. Furthermore, we apply our methodology to a real-world dataset, highlighting its practical implications and potential for enhancing predictive modeling in survival analysis. Our results indicate that the Bayesian approach significantly improves parameter estimation and uncertainty quantification compared to traditional methods, making it a valuable tool for researchers and practitioners dealing with phase-type distributions in the presence of covariates.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: In the realm of cryptography, the security of stream ciphers relies heavily on the unpredictability and randomness of the generated keystreams. This paper introduces a novel statistical approach for assessing the randomness of stream cipher outputs by employing the concept of the binary derivative. The binary derivative reflects the rate of change between consecutive bits in a binary sequence, allowing for a nuanced analysis of bit correlation and information flow. We develop a rigorous framework to compute the binary derivative for keystreams produced by various widely-used stream ciphers and apply a series of statistical tests to evaluate their randomness characteristics. Through extensive simulations and empirical validation, we establish benchmarks for the expected behavior of the binary derivative in truly random sequences versus those generated by stream ciphers. Our findings indicate that deviations in the binary derivative can serve as effective indicators of potential weaknesses in the keystream, thereby providing a unique tool for cryptanalysts and security professionals. This research not only contributes to the field of cryptographic analysis but also paves the way for further study into alternative randomness testing methodologies for cryptographic systems.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: Model choice plays an increasingly important role in statistics. From a Bayesian perspective a crucial goal is to compute the marginal likelihood of the data for a given model. However, this is typically a difficult task since it amounts to integrating over all model parameters. The aim of the paper is to illustrate how this may be achieved by using ideas from thermodynamic integration or path sampling. We show how the marginal likelihood can be computed via Markov chain Monte Carlo methods on modified posterior distributions for each model. This then allows Bayes factors or posterior model probabilities to be calculated. We show that this approach requires very little tuning and is straightforward to implement. The new method is illustrated in a variety of challenging statistical settings.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: A Bayesian approach to modelling binary data on a regular lattice is introduced. The method uses a hierarchical model where the observed data is the sign of a hidden conditional autoregressive Gaussian process. This approach essentially extends the familiar probit model to dependent data. Markov chain Monte Carlo simulations are used on real and simulated data to estimate the posterior distribution of the spatial dependency parameters and the method is shown to work well. The method can be straightforwardly extended to regression models.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus Aureus (MRSA) is a pathogen that continues to be of major concern in hospitals. We develop models and computational schemes based on observed weekly incidence data to estimate MRSA transmission parameters. We extend the deterministic model of McBryde, Pettitt, and McElwain (2007, Journal of Theoretical Biology 245, 470-481) involving an underlying population of MRSA colonized patients and health-care workers that describes, among other processes, transmission between uncolonized patients and colonized health-care workers and vice versa. We develop new bivariate and trivariate Markov models to include incidence so that estimated transmission rates can be based directly on new colonizations rather than indirectly on prevalence. Imperfect sensitivity of pathogen detection is modeled using a hidden Markov process. The advantages of our approach include (i) a discrete valued assumption for the number of colonized health-care workers, (ii) two transmission parameters can be incorporated into the likelihood, (iii) the likelihood depends on the number of new cases to improve precision of inference, (iv) individual patient records are not required, and (v) the possibility of imperfect detection of colonization is incorporated. We compare our approach with that used by McBryde et al. (2007) based on an approximation that eliminates the health-care workers from the model, uses Markov chain Monte Carlo and individual patient data. We apply these models to MRSA colonization data collected in a small intensive care unit at the Princess Alexandra Hospital, Brisbane, Australia.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: In this paper we develop multiple case deletion statistics for the general linear model so that a,residual vector and a leverage matrix are identified which have roles analogous to residuals and leverage for ordinary least squares models. We extend the notion of the conditional deletion diagnostic to general linear models. The residuals, leverage and deletion diagnostics are illustrated with data modelled by a linear growth curve.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: We consider the problem of adapting weighted least squares estimation so that estimates can be found with censored or grouped data. The EM algorithm is implemented for the linear model where the errors are assumed to be generated by a scale mixture of normal distributions. In particular, explicit results are given for the case where the marginal distribution of the error is Student-t with an even number of degrees of freedom. Expressions for the observed information are found, relating grouped data results to those for right censored data. Some ad hoc rules for the identification of outliers are given. An example involving the lifetimes of motorettes is considered.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: We consider the investigation of time dependence in Cox's proportional hazards model using the residuals of Schoenfeld. For data analysis and model development we consider smoothing these residuals to consider time-dependent effects. A model which considers time-dependent modulation of the linear predictor is introduced and suggested for use. The techniques are illustrated using simulated data and data concerning the failure response, measured as distance travelled, of turbochargers on railway carriages. For the latter case, a time'-dependent proportional hazards model of this type is suggested by smoothing the residuals and it is shown to give an improved fit to the data.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: Discrete Markov random field models provide a natural framework for representing images or spatial datasets. They model the spatial association present while providing a convenient Markovian dependency structure and strong edge-preservation properties. However, parameter estimation for discrete Markov random field models is difficult due to the complex form of the associated normalizing constant for the likelihood function. For large lattices, the reduced dependence approximation to the normalizing constant is based on the concept of performing computationally efficient and feasible forward recursions on smaller sublattices, which are then suitably combined to estimate the constant for the entire lattice. We present an efficient computational extension of the forward recursion approach for the autologistic model to lattices that have an irregularly shaped boundary and that may contain regions with no data; these lattices are typical in applications. Consequently, we also extend the reduced dependence approximation to these scenarios, enabling us to implement a practical and efficient nonsimulation-based approach for spatial data analysis within the variational Bayesian framework. The methodology is illustrated through application to simulated data and example images. The online supplementary materials include our C source code for computing the approximate normalizing constant and simulation studies.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: Indirect inference (II) is a methodology for estimating the parameters of an intractable (generative) model on the basis of an alternative parametric (auxiliary) model that is both analytically and computationally easier to deal with. Such an approach has been well explored in the classical literature but has received substantially less attention in the Bayesian paradigm. The purpose of this paper is to compare and contrast a collection of what we call parametric Bayesian indirect inference (pBII) methods. One class of pBII methods uses approximate Bayesian computation (referred to here as ABC II) where the summary statistic is formed on the basis of the auxiliary model, using ideas from II. Another approach proposed in the literature, referred to here as parametric Bayesian indirect likelihood (pBIL), uses the auxiliary likelihood as a replacement to the intractable likelihood. We show that pBIL is a fundamentally different approach to ABC II. We devise new theoretical results for pBIL to give extra insights into its behaviour and also its differences with ABC II. Furthermore, we examine in more detail the assumptions required to use each pBII method. The results, insights and comparisons developed in this paper are illustrated on simple examples and two other substantive applications. The first of the substantive examples involves performing inference for complex quantile distributions based on simulated data while the second is for estimating the parameters of a trivariate stochastic process describing the evolution of macroparasites within a host based on real data. We create a novel framework called Bayesian indirect likelihood (BIL) that encompasses pBII as well as general ABC methods so that the connections between the methods can be established.

It is shown that the statistics are particularly sensitive to certain kinds of pattern in the data and they could be useful in data analysis apart from providing a formal test of bivariate normality

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: A new variational Bayesian (VB) algorithm, split and eliminate VB (SEVB), for modeling data via a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) is developed. This new algorithm makes use of component splitting in a way that is more appropriate for analyzing a large number of highly heterogeneous spiky spatial patterns with weak prior information than existing VB-based approaches. SEVB is a highly computationally efficient approach to Bayesian inference and like any VB-based algorithm it can perform model selection and parameter value estimation simultaneously. A significant feature of our algorithm is that the fitted number of components is not limited by the initial proposal giving increased modeling flexibility. We introduce two types of split operation in addition to proposing a new goodness-of-fit measure for evaluating mixture models. We evaluate their usefulness through empirical studies. In addition, we illustrate the utility of our new approach in an application on modeling human mobility patterns. This application involves large volumes of highly heterogeneous spiky data; it is difficult to model this type of data well using the standard VB approach as it is too restrictive and lacking in the flexibility required. Empirical results suggest that our algorithm has also improved upon the goodness-of-fit that would have been achieved using the standard VB method, and that it is also more robust to various initialization settings.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: Phase-type distributions represent the time to absorption for a finite state Markov chain in continuous time, generalising the exponential distribution and providing a flexible and useful modelling tool. We present a new reversible jump Markov chain Monte Carlo scheme for performing a fully Bayesian analysis of the popular Coxian subclass of phase-type models: the convenient Coxian representation involves fewer parameters than a more general phase-type model. The key novelty of our approach is that we model covariate dependence in the mean whilst using the Coxian phase-type model as a very general residual distribution. Such incorporation of covariates into the model has not previously been attempted in the Bayesian literature. A further novelty is that we also propose a reversible jump scheme for investigating structural changes to the model brought about by the introduction of Erlang phases. Our approach addresses more questions of inference than previous Bayesian treatments of this model and is automatic in nature. We analyse an example clataset comprising lengths of hospital stays of a sample of patients collected from two Australian hospitals to produce a model for a patient's expected length of stay which incorporates the effects of several covariates. This leads to interesting conclusions about what contributes to length of hospital stay with implications for hospital planning. We compare our results with an alternative classical analysis of these data. (C) 2009 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: In statistical analysis, identifying and testing for specific patterns within subblocks of data plays a critical role in various fields, including genetics, finance, and social sciences. This paper presents a comprehensive framework for testing subblock patterns, characterized by their unique structural features and underlying dependencies. We introduce novel statistical methods tailored to detect both predefined and emerging patterns within subblocks, employing a combination of hypothesis testing, permutation methods, and multivariate regression techniques. Our approach accounts for the heterogeneity of data distributions and allows for adjustments in the presence of confounding variables. We provide theoretical derivations to ensure the robustness and efficacy of our proposed methods, followed by a series of simulations that illustrate their performance compared to existing techniques. Additionally, we apply our methods to real-world datasets, demonstrating their utility in uncovering significant subblock patterns that may have gone undetected. The results underscore the relevance of the proposed methodologies in enhancing pattern recognition in complex datasets, setting a foundation for future research in adaptive statistical modeling and analysis.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: In Bayesian statistics, the estimation of marginal likelihood is fundamental for model comparison and selection. Traditional methods, such as bridge sampling and importance sampling, often encounter challenges due to numerical instability and high computational costs, particularly in high-dimensional parameter spaces. This paper presents a novel approach to marginal likelihood estimation using power posteriors, a technique that interpolates between the prior and the posterior distributions through a power transformation of the likelihood. We derive the theoretical foundation for power posterior methods and demonstrate their capacity to provide robust estimates of marginal likelihood while maintaining computational efficiency. A series of simulations and real-data applications illustrate the effectiveness of our approach in terms of accuracy and scalability. Additionally, we compare our method to existing marginal likelihood estimation techniques, showcasing its advantages in diverse modeling scenarios. The proposed power posterior framework not only enhances our understanding of marginal likelihood but also offers a flexible and powerful tool for Bayesian model practitioners.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: In this paper, we propose a novel spatial modelling framework for binary data based on a Hidden Conditional Autoregressive (CAR) Gaussian Process, extending traditional univariate probit models to accommodate multivariate responses. Our approach leverages the inherent spatial correlation present in binary outcomes, allowing for rich, flexible representations of underlying latent structures. Specifically, we introduce a hierarchical model where the binary observations are governed by a latent Gaussian process that captures spatial dependencies. The parameters of the model are estimated using a Bayesian framework, employing Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) techniques for inference. We assess the model's performance through simulations and apply it to a real-world dataset, demonstrating its efficacy in capturing complex spatial relationships and providing insights into underlying processes driving binary outcomes. Our findings highlight the benefits of incorporating spatial structure in binary data analysis, paving the way for enhanced predictive accuracy and interpretation in various fields such as epidemiology, ecology, and social sciences.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: In recent years, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) has emerged as a significant public health challenge, particularly within hospital settings. This study presents a comprehensive investigation into the transmission dynamics of MRSA in a hospital ward using multivariate Markov process models. We propose a framework that accommodates multiple interconnected pathways of infection spread, including patient-to-patient transmission, contact with contaminated surfaces, and healthcare worker interactions. By employing a multivariate approach, we can capture the complex dependencies between different transmission nodes while accounting for time-varying transitions and varying levels of susceptibility among patients. Using empirical data from a high-acuity medical ward, we calibrate our models to assess key parameters influencing MRSA spread, such as the effectiveness of infection control measures and the impact of patient mobility. Our results highlight the importance of considering multiple transmission routes simultaneously, revealing patterns that single-variable models may overlook. We also discuss implications for hospital infection prevention strategies, providing insights into resource allocation and preventive interventions. This study underscores the value of advanced statistical modeling in understanding and controlling the spread of resistant infections in healthcare environments.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: In the analysis of general linear models, the impact of outliers and influential observations on parameter estimates and model validity is a critical concern. This paper presents a comprehensive framework for multiple and conditional deletion diagnostics aimed at identifying and assessing the influence of such observations. Building on established statistical theory, we propose novel diagnostic tools that extend traditional methods by incorporating conditional analysis to better understand the impact of influential data points within specific subgroups. Our approach employs a combination of robust statistical techniques and computational simulations to evaluate the effectiveness of these diagnostics in detecting outliers under various model specifications. We illustrate the application of our proposed diagnostics through a series of case studies, demonstrating their utility in practical scenarios and their advantages over existing methods. The results show that our multiple and conditional deletion diagnostics significantly enhance model robustness and provide deeper insights into data behavior, ultimately aiding researchers in making more informed decisions when fitting general linear models. This paper advances the field of statistical diagnostics by offering a more nuanced approach to handling influential observations, emphasizing the importance of context in statistical analysis.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: This paper explores the application of added variable plots (AVPs) in the context of time series data characterized by counts, a common feature in various fields such as epidemiology, economics, and environmental studies. Traditional regression diagnostics often rely on residual analysis to assess model fit and identify influential observations; however, the unique challenges posed by count data such as non-negativity, overdispersion, and temporal dependence require tailored approaches. We present a methodological framework for constructing and interpreting added variable plots specifically designed for count time series, which allow researchers to visualize the effect of individual predictors while accounting for the dynamic structure inherent in the data. Through simulation studies and real-world case applications, we demonstrate how these plots can reveal crucial insights into the relationships between predictors and response variables, as well as assist in identifying potential model misspecification. Our findings highlight the utility of AVPs as a complementary diagnostic tool in time series analysis of count data, paving the way for more robust and informative statistical modeling practices.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: In the presence of censored and grouped data, traditional least-squares estimation methods can yield biased results, complicating the inference processes in various statistical applications. This paper introduces a novel re-weighted least-squares estimation technique that effectively accommodates the unique challenges posed by such data structures. We leverage the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm to iteratively refine the parameter estimates, allowing for the proper handling of both censored observations and grouped data. Our method involves an initial estimation step that accounts for data censoring, followed by a re-weighting process that adjusts for the grouping effects. We demonstrate the efficiency and robustness of our approach through comprehensive simulations and a case study in survival analysis. Key performance metrics indicate improved accuracy and convergence relative to existing methods. The proposed framework offers a valuable tool for statisticians dealing with complex datasets and highlights the potential of the EM algorithm in enhancing estimation methods in challenging scenarios.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: In survival analysis, the Cox proportional hazards model is a widely used method for exploring the relationship between covariates and the risk of an event occurring over time. Despite its popularity, the assumption of proportional hazards that the hazard ratios remain constant over time can be restrictive and may lead to biased results if violated. This paper investigates the presence of time-dependence in the Cox model by employing both graphical and statistical methodologies to evaluate the assumption of proportional hazards across various datasets. We apply time-varying covariates and incorporate functional forms of time dependence to capture the dynamic nature of risk. Through extensive simulation studies and real-world applications, we demonstrate the importance of assessing time-dependence in improving model fit and predictive accuracy. Our findings reveal that the incorporation of time-varying effects can significantly alter the interpretation of hazard ratios and lead to more nuanced insights into survival data. We conclude by discussing practical implications for researchers and practitioners in survival analysis and highlight future directions for refining the Cox proportional hazards model to accommodate time-dependent covariates more effectively.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: This paper presents a novel approach to the statistical analysis of the autologistic model using Variational Bayes (VB) techniques combined with the Reduced Dependence Approximation (RDA) for applications on irregular grids. The autologistic model, characterized by its dependence on spatially correlated binary outcomes, is particularly challenging to analyze in non-standard grid structures due to computational complexities. We introduce a variational inference framework that enables efficient estimation of model parameters, leveraging the RDA to mitigate the high-dimensional dependence inherent in the model. Our methodology is evaluated on synthetic datasets and real-world applications, demonstrating improved computational efficiency and accuracy in parameter estimation compared to traditional Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of our findings for spatial data analysis in fields such as ecology and epidemiology, where irregular grid structures are commonplace. The results indicate that the proposed VB and RDA approach is a promising alternative for modeling spatial correlations in binary data, paving the way for future research in this domain.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: This paper presents a novel approach to Bayesian indirect inference by leveraging a parametric auxiliary model to improve the estimation of parameters in complex models. Indirect inference is a robust statistical method that allows for the estimation of parameters by approximating the target model through a simpler auxiliary model whose parameters can be easily derived. In this study, we introduce an innovative Bayesian framework that incorporates a parametric auxiliary model to bridge the gap between latent variables and observable data. Our proposed methodology enhances the traditional indirect inference framework by providing a probabilistic interpretation of the auxiliary model parameters, allowing for more accurate inference and uncertainty quantification. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through a series of Monte Carlo simulations and apply it to real-world datasets, comparing it against standard estimation techniques. Results indicate significant improvements in parameter estimation accuracy and computational efficiency, establishing the utility of Bayesian indirect inference combined with parametric auxiliary modeling in statistical applications. The findings contribute to the growing intersection of Bayesian methods and indirect inference, offering new insights and tools for researchers dealing with complex statistical models.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: In the realm of cryptography, the security of stream ciphers relies heavily on the unpredictability and randomness of the generated keystreams. This paper introduces a novel statistical approach for assessing the randomness of stream cipher outputs by employing the concept of the binary derivative. The binary derivative reflects the rate of change between consecutive bits in a binary sequence, allowing for a nuanced analysis of bit correlation and information flow. We develop a rigorous framework to compute the binary derivative for keystreams produced by various widely-used stream ciphers and apply a series of statistical tests to evaluate their randomness characteristics. Through extensive simulations and empirical validation, we establish benchmarks for the expected behavior of the binary derivative in truly random sequences versus those generated by stream ciphers. Our findings indicate that deviations in the binary derivative can serve as effective indicators of potential weaknesses in the keystream, thereby providing a unique tool for cryptanalysts and security professionals. This research not only contributes to the field of cryptographic analysis but also paves the way for further study into alternative randomness testing methodologies for cryptographic systems.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: Assessing the bivariate normality of data sets is crucial in many statistical applications, including multivariate analysis and regression modeling. Traditional methods for testing normality often rely on parametric assumptions, which may not hold in practice. This paper presents a novel testing procedure for bivariate normality that utilizes the empirical distribution function (EDF). By leveraging the EDF's ability to capture the joint distribution of the observations, we propose a statistic based on the Kolmogorov-Smirnov framework adapted for the bivariate case. The proposed method is evaluated through extensive simulations, demonstrating its robustness against deviations from normality and its superior performance compared to existing tests. We also provide a consistent bootstrap approach to enhance the power of our test when applied to finite sample sizes. Finally, the practical applicability of our method is illustrated through real-world data examples, reinforcing the EDF's effectiveness as a tool for assessing bivariate normality. Our findings contribute to the toolkit available for practitioners facing the challenges of multivariate data analysis.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: In recent years, understanding human mobility patterns has become increasingly essential for various applications, including urban planning, transportation management, and epidemiology. This paper introduces a novel variational Bayesian algorithm designed to improve the modeling of human mobility patterns by efficiently capturing the complexities and uncertainties inherent in human movement data. Leveraging advances in variational inference, our proposed algorithm enhances conventional Bayesian approaches by incorporating adaptive learning mechanisms that tailor posterior approximations to evolving mobility behaviors. We validate our method through extensive simulations and real-world datasets, demonstrating its robustness in identifying latent mobility states and its superior performance over existing algorithms. The results indicate that our approach not only provides more accurate predictions of mobility patterns but also offers insights into the factors influencing human movement. This research contributes to the growing field of mobility modeling and highlights the potential of variational Bayesian methods in addressing complex, data-driven challenges in human behavior analysis.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: In this paper, we propose a fully Bayesian framework for the inference of Coxian phase-type distributions that incorporate covariate-dependent means. Phase-type distributions are widely utilized in various fields, including queuing theory and reliability analysis, due to their flexibility in modeling complex time-to-event data. However, traditional methods often fail to account for the influence of covariates on the distribution parameters. Our approach leverages Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods to posterior sampling, allowing us to integrate covariate effects into the Coxian phase-type structure seamlessly. We develop a prior specification that accommodates the hierarchical nature of the model, enhancing its robustness against overfitting. Through extensive simulation studies, we demonstrate the efficacy of our Bayesian framework in accurately estimating parameters and making predictions in scenarios with varying complexity. Furthermore, we apply our methodology to a real-world dataset, highlighting its practical implications and potential for enhancing predictive modeling in survival analysis. Our results indicate that the Bayesian approach significantly improves parameter estimation and uncertainty quantification compared to traditional methods, making it a valuable tool for researchers and practitioners dealing with phase-type distributions in the presence of covariates.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: In this paper we present a methodology for designing experiments for efficiently estimating the parameters of models with computationally intractable likelihoods. The approach combines a commonly used methodology for robust experimental design, based on Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling, with approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) to ensure that no likelihood evaluations are required. The utility function considered for precise parameter estimation is based upon the precision of the ABC posterior distribution, which we form efficiently via the ABC rejection algorithm based on pre-computed model simulations. Our focus is on stochastic models and, in particular, we investigate the methodology for Markov process models of epidemics and macroparasite population evolution. The macroparasite example involves a multivariate process and we assess the loss of information from not observing all variables.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: Motor unit number estimation (MUNE) is a method which aims to provide a quantitative indicator of progression of diseases that lead to a loss of motor units, such as motor neurone disease. However the development of a reliable, repeatable and fast real-time MUNE method has proved elusive hitherto. Previously, a reversible jump Markov chain Monte Carlo (RJMCMC) algorithm has been implemented to produce a posterior distribution for the number of motor units using a Bayesian hierarchical model that takes into account biological information about motor unit activation. However this approach can be unreliable for some datasets since it can suffer from poor cross-dimensional mixing. The focus is on improved inference by marginalising over latent variables to create the likelihood. More specifically, the emphasis is on how this marginalisation can improve the RJMCMC mixing and that alternative approaches that utilise the likelihood (e.g. DIC) can be investigated. For this model the marginalisation is over latent variables which, for a larger number of motor units, is an intractable summation over all combinations of a set of latent binary variables whose joint sample space increases exponentially with the number of motor units. A tractable and accurate approximation for this quantity is provided and also other approximations based on Monte Carlo estimates that can be incorporated into RJMCMC are investigated. (C) 2013 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: Model choice plays an increasingly important role in statistics. From a Bayesian perspective a crucial goal is to compute the marginal likelihood of the data for a given model. However, this is typically a difficult task since it amounts to integrating over all model parameters. The aim of the paper is to illustrate how this may be achieved by using ideas from thermodynamic integration or path sampling. We show how the marginal likelihood can be computed via Markov chain Monte Carlo methods on modified posterior distributions for each model. This then allows Bayes factors or posterior model probabilities to be calculated. We show that this approach requires very little tuning and is straightforward to implement. The new method is illustrated in a variety of challenging statistical settings.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: The use of Bayesian methodologies for solving optimal experimental design problems has increased. Many of these methods have been found to be computationally intensive for design problems that require a large number of design points. A simulation-based approach that can be used to solve optimal design problems in which one is interested in finding a large number of (near) optimal design points for a small number of design variables is presented. The approach involves the use of lower dimensional parameterisations that consist of a few design variables, which generate multiple design points. Using this approach, one simply has to search over a few design variables, rather than searching over a large number of optimal design points, thus providing substantial computational savings. The methodologies are demonstrated on four applications, including the selection of sampling times for pharmacokinetic and heat transfer studies, and involve nonlinear models. Several Bayesian design criteria are also compared and contrasted, as well as several different lower dimensional parameterisation schemes for generating the many design points. (C) 2013 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: Statistical tests based on the scan statistic are introduced for detecting possible increases in the occurrence of hospital events. The tests use a moving window and the theoretical aspects of the tests are investigated using Markov chain theory. The main objective of this study is to provide a statistical technique to assist hospital staff in deciding whether the variation they observe is greater than usually expected under random variation. In this paper we develop the test for Poisson data and apply the theory to monitor the occurrence of orthopaedic wound infection and Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus colonization. We find that this method is sensitive in detecting the change in the process parameter which may not be detected by standard control chart methods. Both online and retrospective analyses are considered. Copyright (0 2003 John Wiley Sons, Ltd.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: An approximation to marginal rank likelihoods is given and used to make inferences for the linear regression model with censored data. The approximations involve linear rank statistics, adapted for censored data, and estimates of their variance. Various explicit scores are given for right censored data and logistic scores for doubly censored data. Inferences using the approximate rank analysis are compared with inferences using fully and partially parametric techniques on two data sets.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: The binary derivative has been used to measure the randomness of a binary string formed by a pseudorandom number generator for use in cipher systems. In this paper we develop statistical properties of the binary derivative and show that certain types of randomness testing in binary derivatives are equivalent to well-established tests for randomness in the original string. A uniform method of testing randomness in binary strings is described based on using the binary derivative. We show that the new tests are faster and more powerful than several of the well-established tests for randomness.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: This article presents a sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) algorithm that can be used for any one-at-a-time Bayesian sequential design problem in the presence of model uncertainty where discrete data are encountered. Our focus is on adaptive design for model discrimination but the methodology is applicable if one has a different design objective such as parameter estimation or prediction. An SMC algorithm is run in parallel for each model and the algorithm relies on a convenient estimator of the evidence of each model that is essentially a function of importance sampling weights. Methods that rely on quadrature for this task suffer from the curse of dimensionality. Approximating posterior model probabilities in this way allows us to use model discrimination utility functions derived from information theory that were previously difficult to compute except for conjugate models. A major benefit of the algorithm is that it requires very little problem-specific tuning. We demonstrate the methodology on three applications, including discriminating between models for decline in motor neuron numbers in patients suffering from motor neuron disease. Computer code to run one of the examples is provided as online supplementary materials.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: A number of statistical tests have been recommended over the last twenty years for assessing the randomness of long binary strings used in cryptographic algorithms. Several of these tests include methods of examining subblock patterns. These tests are the uniformity test, the universal test and the repetition test. The effectiveness of these tests are compared based on the subblock length, the limitations on data requirements, and on their power in detecting deviations from randomness. Due to the complexity of the test statistics, the power functions are estimated by simulation methods. The results show that for small subblocks the uniformity test is more powerful than the universal test, and that there is some doubt about the parameters of the hypothesised distribution for the universal test statistic. For larger subblocks the results show that the repetition test is the most effective test, since it requires far less data than either of the other two tests and is an efficient test in detecting deviations from randomness in binary strings.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: Bayesian inference has commonly been performed on nonlinear mixed effects models. However, there is a lack of research into performing Bayesian optimal design for nonlinear mixed effects models, especially those that require searches to be performed over several design variables. This is likely due to the fact that it is much more computationally intensive to perform optimal experimental design for nonlinear mixed effects models than it is to perform inference in the Bayesian framework. Fully Bayesian experimental designs for nonlinear mixed effects models are presented, which involve the use of simulation-based optimal design methods to search over both continuous and discrete design spaces. The design problem is to determine the optimal number of subjects and samples per subject, as well as the (near) optimal urine sampling times for a population pharmacokinetic study in horses, so that the population pharmacokinetic parameters can be precisely estimated, subject to cost constraints. The optimal sampling strategies, in terms of the number of subjects and the number of samples per subject, were found to be substantially different between the examples considered in this work, which highlights the fact that the designs are rather problem-dependent and can be addressed using the methods presented. (C) 2015 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: The issue of modelling non-Gaussian time series data is one that has been examined by several authors in recent years. Zeger(1988) introduced a parameter-driven model for a time series of counts as well as a more general observation-driven model for non-Gaussian data (Zeger Qaqish, 1988). This paper examines the application of the added variable plot to these two models. This plot is useful for determining the strength of relationships and the detection of influential or outlying observations.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: We estimate the parameters of a stochastic process model for a macroparasite population within a host using approximate Bayesian computation (ABC). The immunity of the host is an unobserved model variable and only mature macroparasites at sacrifice of the host are counted. With very limited data, process rates are inferred reasonably precisely. Modeling involves a three variable Markov process for which the observed data likelihood is computationally intractable. ABC methods are particularly useful when the likelihood is analytically or computationally intractable. The ABC algorithm we present is based on sequential Monte Carlo, is adaptive in nature, and overcomes some drawbacks of previous approaches to ABC. The algorithm is validated on a test example involving simulated data from an autologistic model before being used to infer parameters of the Markov process model for experimental data. The fitted model explains the observed extra-binomial variation in terms of a zero-one immunity variable, which has a short-lived presence in the host.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: The autologistic model is commonly used to model spatial binary data on the lattice. However, if the lattice size is too large, then exact calculation of its normalizing constant poses a major difficulty. Various different methods for estimation of model parameters, such as pseudo-likelihood, have been proposed to overcome this problem. This article presents a method to estimate the normalizing constant in an efficient manner. In particular, this allows tasks such as maximum likelihood estimation and inference for model parameters. We also consider the true likelihood approximated by the product of likelihoods for which the normalizing constant can be found by an analytic computational method by wrapping the lattice on the cylinder. This gives a simulation-free method of inference. We compare estimates of model parameters based on our new methods with the commonly used pseudo-likelihood approach. Although we have not considered Bayesian inferences here, the method can be straightforwardly extended to find posterior distributions. We apply our methods to the well-known endive data and to simulated data and find that our methods give substantially increased accuracy of estimation of model parameters.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: In this paper, we present new multivariate quantile distributions and utilise likelihood-free Bayesian algorithms for inferring the parameters. In particular, we apply a sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) algorithm that is adaptive in nature and requires very little tuning compared with other approximate Bayesian computation algorithms. Furthermore, we present a framework for the development of multivariate quantile distributions based on a copula. We consider bivariate and time series extensions of the g-and-k distribution under this framework, and develop an efficient component-wise updating scheme free of likelihood functions to be used within the SMC algorithm. In addition, we trial the set of octiles as summary statistics as well as functions of these that form robust measures of location, scale, skewness and kurtosis. We show that these modifications lead to reasonably precise inferences that are more closely comparable to computationally intensive likelihood-based inference. We apply the quantile distributions and algorithms to simulated data and an example involving daily exchange rate returns. (C) 2011 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: In this paper, we explore novel methodologies for Bayesian experimental design in the context of statistical models characterized by intractable likelihoods. Intractable likelihoods, often arising in complex hierarchical models or high-dimensional settings, pose significant challenges to conventional Bayesian inference and design approaches. We propose a framework that integrates surrogate modeling techniques, approximate Bayesian computation, and adaptive sampling strategies to facilitate efficient experimental design when explicit likelihood functions are unavailable. Our approach utilizes existing data to inform prior distributions and leverages simulation-based methods to estimate the marginal likelihood, guiding the selection of experimental conditions that optimize information gain. Through a series of simulation studies and application to real-world case studies, we demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed methods, illustrating improvements in parameter estimation and predictive accuracy compared to traditional design methods. We conclude with recommendations for practitioners facing similar challenges and highlight avenues for future research in Bayesian experimental design under intractable likelihood constraints.

author: Anthony Pettitt
text: In this paper, we present a novel statistical approach that integrates Marginal Reversible Jump Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MRJ-MCMC) techniques for the estimation of motor unit numbers in electrophysiological studies. Traditional methods for assessing motor unit number rely on restrictive assumptions around model parameters, which can lead to biased inferences. Our MRJ-MCMC framework enhances the flexibility of model selection by allowing the number of parameters to change across iterations, thus accommodating varying complexities in the underlying data structure. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by applying it to simulated datasets and real-world electromyographic data. Our results reveal significant improvements in parameter estimation accuracy and uncertainty quantification compared to conventional methods. Additionally, we provide a thorough discussion on the implementation details, including convergence diagnostics and computational considerations. This work not only advances methodologies in motor unit estimation but also contributes to the broader field of Bayesian statistical modeling, offering a versatile tool for researchers analyzing hierarchical and mixed models.
